item.title: Pentagon Agreement With N.I.H. on Biodefense Draws Alarm From Democrats
item.description:
The Pentagon and the National Institutes of Health have signed an agreement to collaborate on biodefense and pandemic preparedness, drawing criticism from Democrats on Capitol Hill who warned that the plan could allow the Defense Department to go around Congress and gain access to billions of dollars meant for infectious disease research.

The agreement, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, is focused on chemical and biological defense research. It does not specify a dollar figure for the partnership or which research projects would be included, but people familiar with it who spoke on the condition of anonymity said it could involve as much as $2 billion from the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, about a third of the agency’s budget.

Congressional Democrats, who publicized the agreement, said they feared it would allow Pentagon officials to spend money lawmakers had allocated for programs at the health agency on their own priorities instead. The Trump administration has repeatedly found ways to go around Congress on spending, including canceling federal grants. It has also used similar arrangements, known as interagency agreements, to try to gut the Education Department by subcontracting its functions to other departments.

“The interagency agreement needs to be terminated immediately,” said Representative Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee. “These funds were provided for lifesaving medical research, not as extra money for the Department of Defense.”

Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, accused the Defense Department of “trying to rob N.I.H. of billions of dollars that Congress provided for medical research so that it can pad the Pentagon’s budget.”

Trump administration officials denied that was the case.

Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, the N.I.H. director, defended the agreement on Friday, writing on social media that “far from siphoning money away from research, this partnership between @NIH and @DeptofWar focuses on research projects that will drive discoveries to improve the health of American citizens and members of the military.”

“Led by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, all work will be 100% aligned with our public health mission,” Mr. Bhattacharya wrote.

Kush Desai, a White House spokesman, said on social media that “the NIH is not transferring any money to the Pentagon. This is a project-by-project research partnership.” He accused Ms. DeLauro of twisting facts about the arrangement to score “political points.”

In a statement, a Pentagon official said that the agreement “represents a significant step forward in protecting the American people and our war fighters,” and “formalizes a productive collaboration” among agencies that Congress had long encouraged.

“The assertion by any official that the agreement was made in secret, or for any other purpose, is false,” the statement said, adding that the deal “does not constitute any blanket transfer of funds.”

The agreement arrives at a moment of turbulence and uncertainty at the infectious disease institute, which has lost many of its longtime leaders and is undergoing major strategic shifts under the Trump administration. The agency is veering away from biodefense and pandemic preparedness research that was once one of its three core areas of focus.

In the journal Nature Medicine this January, N.I.H. leaders set out a new vision for the infectious disease institute, arguing that the agency’s work on pandemic preparedness “clearly neither prevented the pandemic nor prevented Americans from experiencing among the highest levels of all-cause excess mortality in the developed world during that time.”

The infectious disease institute played a leading role in the scientific response to the pandemic, and its longtime director, Dr. Anthony S. Fauci, was the public face of many pandemic policies. The agency was instrumental in the rapid development of vaccines credited with saving millions of lives, but has since become a political lightning rod.

In the past, about a third of the agency’s roughly $6.6 billion budget has been allocated for biodefense and emerging pathogen research. But in a recent strategic plan, the word “biodefense” was absent.

The agreement was signed by Dr. Bhattacharya and Dr. Robert Kadlec at the Defense Department. Dr. Kadlec previously served as assistant secretary for preparedness and response at the Department of Health and Human Services and played a central role in Operation Warp Speed, the federal government’s effort to rapidly develop vaccines and therapeutics against Covid-19.

A spokeswoman for the Department of Health and Human Services, Madeline Meeker, said in a statement that potential collaborations could “support the development of medical technologies, such as therapeutics, diagnostics and personal protective equipment, to protect against infectious diseases and other health risks that Americans face,” citing the response to the Ebola outbreak as an example.

It comes as the Pentagon has sought to significantly increase its budget. The administration has requested $1.5 trillion, including a $350 billion tranche of funding passed through the partisan reconciliation process.

Both requests are stalled on Capitol Hill. Democrats opposed to the war in Iran have refused to provide more funding to the Pentagon through the bipartisan appropriations process, and Senate Republicans remain divided over the budget plan needed to start the reconciliation process.

Congressional Republicans last year included $150 billion in additional funding for the Pentagon in their major tax and spending cuts legislation.

Helene Cooper contributed reporting.

item.title: Homeland Security Dept. Asks for Inquiries Into Voting Machines
item.description:
Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, has asked the Justice Department to examine whether a commonly used voting machine can be trusted to create a verifiable record, in what appeared to be the Trump administration’s latest effort to cast doubt on digital voting systems.

In a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche on Wednesday, Mr. Mullin asked the Justice Department to determine whether devices that tally votes through bar codes or QR codes provided what he described as a “reliable record for a manual audit.”

The letter, which asked Mr. Blanche for his department’s help in ensuring that machines known as ballot-marking devices comply with federal law, raises questions about whether the request sought to lay the ground for claiming that some electronically cast or counted votes are invalid.

Unlike the process of voting by handwritten ballot, ballot-marking devices rely on ballots printed from a touch-screen computer. The ballots, which typically designate a voter’s choice in text form and in a bar code or QR code, are then fed into a separate machine that reads the information.

Critics of the devices have claimed that hackers could in theory manipulate the digital codes, though election integrity experts say there are no examples of that happening in an election. The devices have been widely used in states like Georgia and South Carolina, where Mr. Trump has won elections.

Election machines are already heavily monitored and regulated through testing and certification by federal agencies, states, local election offices and private labs. (The Trump administration recently forced out the independent members of the Election Assistance Commission, which oversees the certification of machines.)

In his letter to Mr. Blanche, Mr. Mullin asked the Justice Department to investigate another pillar of the country’s election infrastructure: a multistate partnership called the Electronic Registration Information Center, or ERIC.

ERIC, a database-sharing consortium that helps states ensure that people vote in only one location, was once considered a wonky, bipartisan initiative to help states clean their voter rolls. But in recent years, it has become a target of election conspiracy theorists trying to sow doubt in the process of administering elections.

In his letter, Mr. Mullin indicated that the requests had initially been made to the Justice Department under his predecessor, Kristi Noem, who was ousted in March. The letter, which congratulated Mr. Blanche on being confirmed as attorney general last month, appeared to be an attempt to nudge him into action less than 60 days before the midterm elections.

The Department of Homeland Security said it had no comment beyond Mr. Mullin’s letter.

President Trump has long complained about electronic voting systems, falsely claiming that they were used in a sprawling plot to rig the 2020 election against him. In March 2025, just two months after he returned to the White House, he issued an executive order in which he “raised the issue of the security of voting systems that rely on bar codes and QR codes,” Mr. Mullin noted in his letter.

Mr. Trump reprised his attacks against these machines in a prime-time address two months ago, saying they were “vulnerable” and “easily compromised.” The president pointed to a trove of declassified intelligence documents to make his case, especially those related to a technology company called Smartmatic, which he said had ties to the Venezuelan government.

But Mr. Trump’s claims about Smartmatic’s devices far outran the problems with them that were described in the declassified materials. One of the documents, a C.I.A. analysis, said that while the Venezuelan government had “some capability in manipulating electronic voting systems,” neither it nor Smartmatic could “manipulate the outcome of an election outside Venezuela.”

Mr. Mullin’s letter did not mention Smartmatic by name. But it did refer to an effort last winter by senior Trump intelligence officials to examine the vulnerabilities of machines built by another company, Dominion Voting Systems, now known as Liberty Vote, which has also been at the center of outlandish conspiracy theories.

Conspiracy theories have also long underpinned the conservative efforts to dismantle ERIC. In the aftermath of the 2020 election, election deniers successfully pressured secretaries of state in many Republican states to withdraw from ERIC, claiming it was a front for left-wing groups to organize voter-registration drives.

Those claims were largely promoted by Heather Honey, then a researcher and activist who is now a top official at the Department of Homeland Security working with Cleta Mitchell, a conservative lawyer who played a role in Mr. Trump’s attempts to overturn the 2020 election. Ms. Honey presented a report to several Republican secretaries of state in the summer of 2022 claiming ERIC was inappropriately influenced by partisan Democrats and left-wing groups.

As a result, nine Republican-led states withdrew from ERIC. But nearly 30 states now still use the system.

ERIC is currently the only system that can reliably catch whether people vote in more than one state. And election officials widely agree that it also helps to identify dead people on voting lists.

Mr. Mullin’s letter suggested that data from ERIC, including “protected motor vehicle data,” had been with an organization called the Center for Election Innovation and Research, a nonpartisan group that works to build confidence in elections. Mr. Mullin told Mr. Blanche that sharing such information with a nongovernmental organization could violate federal privacy laws.

The Center for Election Innovation and Research is run by David Becker, a former voting rights lawyer for the Justice Department who also helped to found the ERIC system. Mr. Becker has vehemently criticized the Trump administration’s attempts to interfere with elections, raising questions about whether the request to investigate ERIC was also an effort to target him and his group.

Mr. Becker said in a statement on Friday that the allegation from Mr. Mullin likely related to research his organization performed over five years ago. Mr. Becker also rejected claims made by Mr. Mullin that the organization received motor vehicle or voter data on an ongoing basis.

“There have been multiple public documents published as far back as early 2022 relating to this research,” the statement said, adding that no one from the Department of Homeland Security contacted the center for “information or clarification” before Mr. Mullin issued his letter.

item.title: Supreme Court Sides With Republicans in TV Ad Fight
item.description:
In a victory for Republicans in the run-up to the midterms, the Supreme Court on Friday found that political parties are entitled to the same low-cost TV ad rates as candidates.

The ruling focused on an obscure but crucial part of political campaign funding that has given Democrats an advantage in recent years.

The court’s majority found that Republican Party committees were likely to suffer “irreparable harm” unless the justices cleared the way for them to receive the low-cost ad rates, saying that requiring party committees to pay more for advertising would hamper “their efforts to reach the electorate in the critical weeks leading up to the midterms.”

The majority added that such an injury “implicates their First Amendment rights to speak and coordinate their political activities freely.”

As is typical in such emergency applications, the order did not include a vote count. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, one of the court’s liberals, dissented.

Republican leaders praised the court’s ruling.

A spokesman for the National Republican Congressional Committee, Will Kiley, called the decision “a win for candidates, parties and broadcasters who have relied on the same rules for years.”

He added: “Democrats can’t win at the ballot box, so they ran to the courthouse in the final weeks of an election to try to limit protected party speech.”

Democratic counterparts pushed back against Friday’s ruling.

A joint statement from senior officials with Democrats’ congressional campaign committees called the Republicans’ move “a concerted effort by Donald Trump and national Republicans to flood the midterm elections with money from billionaire donors.” The officials, Devan Barber and Will Van Nuys, added that Republicans were seeking to “drown out the power of the grass roots because they know their agenda is deeply unpopular and they cannot win on the merits.”

The dispute focuses on the 1971 Federal Election Campaign Act, which set out rules for how broadcasting stations must interact with political candidates during election seasons.

The federal law requires broadcasters to give political candidates low rates to buy TV ad time in the weeks before an election — a key way to reach voters. Before the court’s ruling, party committees had not been able to take advantage of those same low rates. That distinction had traditionally benefited Democrats, whose candidates tend to raise more money than their committees. The opposite is true for Republicans.

Republicans have pushed for ways to undo this advantage, notably in a Supreme Court case last term in which Republican groups successfully argued to lift coordinated spending limits between political parties and candidates.

In late June, in a 6-to-3 decision split along ideological lines, the justices sided with Republicans.

With a decision in their favor, Republicans had planned to coordinate with candidates to buy up TV ad time under the lower rates.

But four Democratic candidates from the battleground states of Georgia, Michigan, North Carolina and Ohio brought a separate but related legal challenge to the lower ad rates.

Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina and Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan together challenged a notice by the Federal Communications Commission, the government agency that regulates broadcasters, that had alerted political parties and committees that they would now be entitled to the low rates.

On Aug. 25, a divided three-judge panel from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit sided with the Democratic challengers. Judge Robert B. King, an appointee of President Bill Clinton, wrote for the majority that the statute was “unambiguous” that only political candidates, not parties, are entitled to the low advertising rates. He added that the F.C.C. notice represented a “significant and unilateral expansion” of the rule.

In dissent, Judge J. Harvie Wilkinson III, an appointee of President Ronald Reagan, wrote that the appeals court’s decision represented “nothing less than an upending of settled campaign finance ground rules right in the middle of an election season.”

National Republican groups then filed an emergency application to the Supreme Court asking the justices to step in and clear the way for them to get the lower ad rates. The Republican challengers argued that the lower court judges had — “in the midst of election season” — rewritten “longstanding rules about preferential broadcast rates for political ads.”

Lawyers for the Trump administration joined them, asking the court to immediately overturn the lower court’s ruling. Solicitor General D. John Sauer asserted that despite the Democratic candidates’ claims that the new F.C.C. guideline would harm them, the new notice in fact did not favor candidates of either party.

In response, lawyers for the Democratic candidates argued that the federal agency action meant they were “facing imminent, irreparable harm.”

Shane Goldmacher contributed reporting.

item.title: Fake Version of Republican Midterm Convention Website Redirects to Epstein Files
item.description:
Someone is very intent on making sure voters don’t forget about the Epstein files.

Republicans eager to find out more about the party’s first-of-its-kind midterm convention in Dallas next week got a surprise this week: a website that initially purported to be the Republican National Committee’s official convention page but then redirected to the Justice Department’s library of files related to Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted sex offender.

It wasn’t a hack. The real convention site, at gopconvention.com, remains operational, prominently featuring an outline of Texas and this bold claim: “The Golden Age of America Has Just Begun.”

Some users searching for the site on Google, however, were directed to an impostor website — at gopdallas2026.com — that earned a spot much higher in search results than the real site.

Google’s preview of the fake page promises “details about the 2026 RNC Midterm Convention at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, Sept. 9-10 including registration, VIP experiences.”

It does not deliver anything of the sort. Instead, a click on the site takes the user to “justice.gov/epstein,” something of a headache for Republicans and President Trump, whose ties to Mr. Epstein have angered the MAGA base and served as an ongoing irritant in an election year expected to be a referendum on his presidency.

The R.N.C. said it believed a creative agency with Democratic ties was behind the fake site, pointing to a Daily Mail article published Friday that cited a Republican opposition research firm’s digital forensic analysis.

“Democrats are too broke to have their own midterm convention, so they settled for a sad, fake little website,” Zach Parkinson, a spokesman for the R.N.C., said in a statement.

Data from an internet registration database, ICANN, showed that the domain was registered on July 7 and updated on Sept. 3. An archived version of the fake site shows that it appeared for weeks as a more straight-ahead impostor of the actual Republican convention site, leading with fireworks, a photo of Mr. Trump and the title “The Great American Comeback Midterm Convention.” It even included a list of potential speakers, such as Mr. Trump and various cabinet secretaries.

The Daily Mail article said that when a reporter reached out to the founder of the Democratic agency, Yosi Sargent, on Thursday, the fake site switched to the Epstein files redirect.

On Friday evening, Mr. Sargent appeared to acknowledge he was behind the site in a text message to The New York Times.

“We made you look,” he wrote. “Satire is such an important art form to draw attention to important issues, like the Epstein files.”

The spoof tricked people for weeks, with news outlets initially citing information it presented and some reporters filing for credentials on the fake website.

“If you were a reporter who submitted a request for credentials through this website and are now left stranded, you now know who screwed you over,” Mr. Parkinson said.

The fake site did include a disclaimer: “This website is an independent informational resource and is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or operated by the Republican National Committee (RNC), the 2026 RNC Midterm Convention, the American Airlines Center, or any official convention entity.”

As recently as Aug. 27, gopdallas2026.com still showed the duplicate site and was not linking to the Epstein files. Nearly 140 other websites linked to it, including The Dallas Morning News, the conservative Daily Wire news site and the New Jersey Federation of Republican Women.

At some point after that date, the site began redirecting to the Epstein files.

Kate Conger contributed reporting.

item.title: In Complex Cases, Consensus Can Be Hard to Reach
item.description:
As Lindsay Clancy’s murder trial came to an end on Friday, there was no shortage of drama.

The courthouse in Plymouth, Mass., was thronged with observers. Ms. Clancy’s lawyer butted heads with the judge and made a doomed appeal to prevent the declaration of a mistrial. Audience members gasped.

But the most pivotal decision took place behind closed doors. After spending nearly 40 hours in deliberation — and half of those in deadlock — jurors said they could not come to a unanimous verdict on whether Ms. Clancy should be held criminally responsible for strangling her three children in 2023. A single juror was said to be at odds with everyone else in the room.

It was a remarkable outcome, said Valerie Hans, a Cornell law professor who studies jury behavior. “Hung juries are not frequent,” she added. “Maybe one out of every 20 cases in criminal courts results in a hung jury.”

Jury verdicts in serious criminal cases across the United States must be unanimous, a rule that was affirmed in a 2020 Supreme Court decision interpreting the Sixth Amendment of the Constitution.

“It’s entirely an artifact of history and tradition,” said Christopher Slobogin, a law professor at Vanderbilt University. He added that the standards for criminal cases were high because a guilty verdict could result in a deprivation of liberty.

Dr. Hans says that failures of consensus are most likely in cases where the evidence is close — that is, not clearly favoring either side — and complex.

The Clancy trial seemed to fit those parameters. Jurors sat through four weeks of emotional, often harrowing, testimony. They watched expert witnesses reach opposite conclusions on Ms. Clancy’s criminal culpability in the death of her children. Her lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argued for an insanity defense, claiming that she had been in the throes of postpartum psychosis.

The jurors, nine women and three men, wore increasingly grim expressions as their deadlock dragged on, even after the judge, William Sullivan, delivered a set of instructions on Wednesday known as the “dynamite charge” in a last-ditch effort to nudge them toward a verdict.

Professor Slobogin said it was notable that Judge Sullivan’s efforts had failed. “Typically, if there is a hung jury, the judge is able to convince the jury to go back and reach a unanimous verdict,” he said.

But on Friday, the jurors said in a note to the court that “with a heavy heart,” they had been unable to reach a consensus.

According to Dr. Hans, the jurors probably took their work very seriously. “People can be very flippant outside the jury context,” she said, “and yet there’s something about getting sworn in as a juror that is sobering.”

That extends beyond the courthouse, she added: Research suggests that people who serve on juries tend to become more civically engaged after the trial ends.

For now, the jurors’ work at the Plymouth courthouse is done. Ms. Clancy still faces murder charges, and prosecutors will decide whether to try their case all over again.

If they do, a brand-new jury will be sworn in.

item.title: Tetris Owner Denounces Trump White House Clone of Game
item.description:
The Tetris Company, the company that owns the rights to the classic video game, denounced a clone of the game produced by the Trump administration that has the player block space aliens and zombies from crossing the U.S.-Mexican border.

It was the latest incident in which an owner of a creative work objected to the Trump administration’s use of it.

Build the Wall, the White House version of Tetris, urges the player to “protect the border from the incoming horde,” which is rhetoric that President Trump and members of his administration often use about immigrants.

“The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of ‘Build the Wall,’” the company said in a statement on social media, adding that “at Tetris we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them. To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we’re grateful to have you in our community.”

On Thursday, the White House shared a page on its official government website that featured five simple video games that promoted Trump administration policies. They are clones of existing games, and the Tetris clone is called Build the Wall with the subtitle Zombie Border Siege. Another game called Rio Run is a clone of the Snake game, where players catch and imprison an increasingly long line of immigrants on the southern border.

Tetris is a puzzle game. Blocks of different shapes fall down the screen and must be sorted into complete lines as they fill up the screen, gradually accelerating. The game was created by Alexey Pajitnov, a Soviet software engineer, in 1984. The Tetris Company continues to license many variants of the game, some of which are marketed to children with Nintendo cartoon characters like Mario, Kirby and Donkey Kong.

Build the Wall has those blocks take the form of the southern border wall, physically blocking aliens and zombies that explode when they collide with the wall.

In its statement, the Tetris Company added, “P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously.”

The Tetris Company won a significant copyright case in 2012 against a company that made a Tetris clone, a ruling that reinforced that the owner of a video game could protect the “look and feel” of the game under copyright law.

A social media video accompanying the White House games also invoked Sega, the creators of Sonic the Hedgehog. The intro to the video includes an image mimicking the company’s logo, a recording of the company’s name being sung and a copyrighted song from the Sonic games.

A long list of musicians have denounced Mr. Trump using their music at his rallies, and some have taken legal action to protect their copyrighted material. In November, the musician Olivia Rodrigo, who is Filipino American, condemned the use of her music in a post by the Department of Homeland Security promoting the Trump administration’s mass deportation effort, writing underneath the post: “don’t ever use my songs to promote your racist, hateful propaganda.”

Trump administration social media posts have sometimes sought to appeal specifically to gamers, especially young men who voted for Mr. Trump in 2024.

One noteworthy post in October by the Department of Homeland Security equated immigrants to the flesh-eating aliens known as “the Flood” in the Halo video game series. The post, which featured an image from the game of a machine-gun armed vehicle, included the caption: “destroy the Flood” with a link to the recruiting website for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Microsoft, which owns Halo, said in a statement at the time that the company “does not have anything to share on this matter.”

item.title: ‘This Is My Money’: Trump Says He Will Spend Some of His War Chest on Republicans
item.description:
President Trump said Friday he plans to spend “probably” $400 million to $500 million on midterm election races, but added that he also intends to hold back resources as Republicans openly beg him to stop sitting on his money and give them financial support.

“This is my money that I control,” Mr. Trump told reporters at the White House. At the same time, he said he believes Republicans can do well in November and he will help.

“I’m going to spend whatever amount of money is necessary,” he said.

As his party struggles to maintain control of Congress, Mr. Trump has been criticized from within his own party as tightfisted.

The president told reporters he estimated he has “like close to a billion dollars” to spend on politics, a total that perhaps includes Republican National Committee funds and money in Mr. Trump’s campaign account. Federal Election Commission documents show that MAGA Inc., Mr. Trump’s political action committee, has about $403 million on hand.

This year, Mr. Trump has spent money to help another candidate once, boosting Senator Darline Graham of South Carolina through last month’s Republican primary in what most political observers view as a safe state for Republicans.

But Republicans in other states are in much more danger of falling to Democrats. The G.O.P. is at risk of losing the House and, to a lesser degree, the Senate, dragged down by Mr. Trump’s low approval ratings. While some candidates have attempted to distance themselves from the president, most are still hoping that Mr. Trump will come through with financial support for their races.

“I’m going to be making contributions to various campaigns of people that I think are good, Republicans that I think are good,” he said.

Even so, Mr. Trump said he planned to save some of his funds for races that are still two years off.

“I expect to have money left over, and we can use that for ’28,” he said.

item.title: Judge Once Again Blocks Mail-In Ballot Rules
item.description:
A federal judge in Boston ruled for the third time on Friday that the Trump administration’s plans to restrict mail-in voting are likely unconstitutional and it should be prevented from implementing them ahead of the midterm election.

Judge Indira Talwani had already temporarily blocked the U.S. Postal Service from moving forward, in a ruling that was set to expire Sept. 10. The new order extends that block indefinitely.

She wrote that the Trump administration appeared to be denying that its effort at the Postal Service was “an election rule” to get around that the Constitution reserves the power to administer elections to the states and Congress.

“This denial rings hollow,” she wrote. “The final rule explicitly and exclusively regulates election mail.”

What the ruling did not do was move the issue much closer to a resolution, even with time rapidly running out for state election officials to start distributing mail-in ballots to voters. The Trump administration had already appealed her temporary block to the Supreme Court, and the justices are likely to have the final word on President Trump’s plans ahead of the election.

The Trump administration filed an appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit less than two hours later.

The ruling came just a day after Judge Talwani held a two-hour hearing in Boston, with lawyers representing large coalitions of Democratic-led states and voting rights groups squared off with lawyers representing the Postal Service and a smaller group of Republican-led states that support the rule.

Judge Talwani reviewed their concerns about the Postal Service rule, which would require states to report to the Postal Service which of their voters are qualified to use mail-in ballots, and to adopt a new ballot envelope designed to be scanned and linked to voters. The Postal Service could withhold mail delivery of ballots in states that don’t comply.

She said she believed the concerns among states and election officials that it was too late to adopt the changes without widespread mishaps and delays. The election is now only 60 days away.

Judge Talwani wrote the rule appeared to force states to work against their own privacy laws and imposed requirements that appeared certain to result in some voters being disqualified.

“Having considered this series of hurdles for officials against the backdrop of an impending election, and mindful of the fact that any minor malfunction will result in the denial of mail ballots, the court concludes that disenfranchisement for plaintiff organizations’ members, regardless of residence, is practically inevitable,” Judge Talwani wrote.

In particular, Judge Talwani questioned why the Postal Service was moving ahead with exceptional urgency to get the rule approved in time for the midterms while also insisting it was a relatively routine action that required only minor clerical changes. She also cast doubt on Mr. Trump’s claims that the rule was necessary for election security.

She wrote that proceeding so soon before the election “threatens disenfranchisement of millions of United States citizens who seek to vote by mail.”

“And, on the other side,” she wrote, she found that “the record includes no evidence relating to fraudulent mail voting to support the rushed implementation.”

Several officials from Democratic-led states welcomed the ruling.

“We are glad that this court has stopped the Postal Service from impacting who can receive a ballot in the 2026 election,” Jena Griswold, Colorado’s secretary of state, said in a statement. “The Postal Service must stick to its job of delivering the mail, rather than trying to decide who gets to vote.”

Still, Judge Talwani wrote that she would not second guess or seek to prevent any of a number of Republican-led states that support the rule from meeting its requirements voluntarily. She also said the decision on Friday addressed only the implementation of the rule for the current election cycle, and that courts could later sort out whether it was lawful in its entirety.

Like in her two previous rulings, she wrote that the rule appeared to exceed the Postal Service’s statutory authority by assigning broad authority to the service to regulate election mail, beyond what lawmakers intended. She added that with each passing week, it had become increasingly unrealistic to expect states to be able to comply.

Jeff Jackson, the North Carolina attorney general, said in a statement that the administration’s request to the Supreme Court on Thursday came just as the state was scheduled to send out ballots to voters on Friday.

“That would throw our election into chaos,” Mr. Jackson said. “The ballots are printed, the process is underway, and North Carolinians deserve a lawful and orderly election.”

The decision on Friday technically appeared to render the Trump administration’s appeals of Judge Talwani’s previous orders moot.

But at the hearing on Thursday, Michael Velchik, a Justice Department attorney representing the Postal Service, indicated that if she took this step, the Trump administration would likely return to the Supreme Court to “start the process again.”

Nicholas Corasaniti contributed reporting.

item.title: C.D.C. Says No Deaths This Year Attributed to Measles
item.description:
Escalating a political fight over two deaths in Pennsylvania, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said on Friday that it did not have any records to indicate “measles is the underlying cause” of any deaths in the country this year.

The phrasing on its website, part of the agency’s weekly update to measles tallies, is the latest development in a heated disagreement between state and federal officials over whether the two deaths were a result of measles or merely coincided with the infection. The dispute echoes similar quarrels over causes of death during the coronavirus pandemic.

The C.D.C.’s update came even as the coroner for Lancaster County, where the deaths reportedly occurred, announced on Friday that a 6-week-old child in the county had died from measles. The child, who died last month, had a rare genetic disorder called Amish microcephaly, according to the coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni.

The Department of Health and Human Services directed a request for comment to a social media post by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

“The facts emerging now demonstrate why C.D.C. waited for the evidence rather than allowing political grandstanding to dictate its reporting,” Mr. Kennedy said in the post.

Infants with Amish microcephaly typically live only about six months, and the infant in question died at approximately 2 months old, the secretary said.

Pennsylvania has been at the center of a rapidly escalating measles outbreak. Nearly 600 people have contracted the disease in the state, and nearly 100 have been hospitalized. Nationwide, the number of measles cases this year has topped 3,000, the highest in 35 years.

Last week, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, a Democrat, announced the two deaths in his state and said the federal government was partly to blame for hesitancy surrounding measles vaccinations. The following day, Mr. Kennedy accused the governor of taking “giddy delight” in announcing the deaths and suggested the reports might have been “fabricated by one of the Governor’s hopeful staffers.”

In its measles update last week, the C.D.C. added an asterisked statement that the “available information does not establish” whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths in Pennsylvania and that the agency needed to review further information.

The New York Times reported on Monday that the C.D.C.’s new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, had ordered agency officials to challenge Pennsylvania’s reporting of the two deaths, shunning the agency’s normal procedure of accepting data shared by states and amplifying the comments by Mr. Kennedy, who is her boss.

The C.D.C.’s update this week retains the asterisk under the death tally but makes no reference to Pennsylvania’s reports. The agency instead says that its National Center for Health Statistics “does not currently have any death records” indicating measles as a cause of death and that it will update its numbers as more information becomes available.

item.title: Trump’s Latest Clemency Grants Benefit Drug Offenders, Union Boss
item.description:
President Trump issued 30 clemency grants on Thursday, including to a drug dealer-turned-business executive, a longtime Philadelphia union boss convicted of bribery and a former Navy sailor imprisoned for firearms offenses.

The clemency grants were confirmed by White House officials and representatives for the recipients.

They went to an eclectic group, continuing Mr. Trump’s unpredictable and unorthodox use of pardons that wipe away most consequences of convictions and commutations, which cut short sentences.

While other presidents have drawn criticism for using clemency to reward supporters or protect allies, Mr. Trump has taken it to a new level. His use of clemency has spawned a cottage industry of lawyers and lobbyists offering to use their connections to bring cases to his attention in exchange for hefty fees.

Thursday’s beneficiaries included some prominent figures. But the pardons also encompassed lower-profile people who were facing long sentences and lacked obvious connections to the president or his allies.

Among them was Holly Leanne Frantzen, who had served more than a decade of a nearly 17-year sentence for drug charges. The White House did not indicate whether she had received a pardon or a commutation.

In a statement pleading for clemency on the website of a prisoners’ rights group, Ms. Frantzen admitted to past struggles with drug addiction. But she indicated that she was working on completing an apprenticeship in plumbing, and that her rehabilitation behind bars had “compelled me to believe that there is hope.”

Alice Marie Johnson, the White House pardon czar, who has focused on elevating the cases of women and nonviolent drug offenders, highlighted Ms. Frantzen in a statement Friday announcing the clemency grants.

“My prayer is that each of these 30 people makes the most of this extraordinary second chance and becomes a greater blessing to their families, communities and the world,” Ms. Johnson said in a post on social media.

Mr. Trump also pardoned Emory Clash Jones, who served more than a decade in prison for a conviction related to selling crack cocaine.

A longtime associate of the rapper Jay-Z’s, Mr. Jones has been out of prison since 2010, according to Bureau of Prisons records. He has worked as an executive at Roc Nation, Jay-Z’s sprawling company.

In her statement, Ms. Johnson praised Mr. Jones as “an entrepreneur and creative leader whose journey reminds us how much people can grow — and how much good they can still do.”

In a letter to the judge overseeing the case in 2009, Jay-Z, writing under his given name Shawn Carter, indicated that he had known Mr. Jones for 15 years, and urged his release, praising his “intelligence, interpersonal skills and solid work ethic.”

Mr. Jones and Roc Nation did not respond to requests for comment.

Another clemency grant went to John Dougherty, who led a Philadelphia-based unit of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers for nearly three decades until he resigned in 2021 after he was convicted of bribing a City Council member there.

Mr. Dougherty, who is known as “Johnny Doc” and had exerted outsized influence in Philadelphia politics for decades, had served less than two years of a six-year prison sentence. The remainder of the sentence was wiped away by a commutation issued by Mr. Trump.

A White House official, who requested anonymity to discuss the president’s clemency decisions, said that Mr. Dougherty’s sentence was commuted to allow him to care for his terminally ill wife. Her father had been caring for her, but he passed away while Mr. Dougherty was in prison, the official said.

George Bochetto, a lawyer for Mr. Dougherty, said in an email on Friday that his client had been released from prison and was headed to Philadelphia “to be by his wife’s side.”

A pardon was granted to Patrick Adamiak, a former sailor who was sentenced in 2023 to 20 years in prison for possessing and selling illegal firearms from his home in Virginia.

The case of Mr. Adamiak, who goes by “Tate,” was championed by gun rights backers who supported Mr. Trump. They argued that his conviction was the result of unclear regulations and a frame job by a confidential informant.

Adam Kraut, the executive director of the Second Amendment Foundation, said in a statement that the case was “every gun owner’s worst nightmare.” Mr. Kraut added that “while Tate shouldn’t have endured what happened to him in the first place, we are thrilled he has finally received the pardon he deserves.”

item.title: North Carolina Adds New Restrictions to Vote-by-Mail Program
item.description:
The North Carolina State Board of Elections added new restrictions to its vote-by-mail program on Friday morning, making it easier for local election officials across the state to discard ballots.

Just hours after counties in the state began sending the nation’s first batch of mail ballots for the fall election, the five-member state board, which is controlled by Republicans, split on party lines to approve the changes. The new rule requires officials to disqualify ballots with an unsealed envelope and limits who can drop off mail ballots on behalf of another voter.

The changes are almost certain to cause some votes to be tossed. They come at a time when President Trump and his allies have repeatedly promoted false claims of widespread fraud in mail voting, and used those false claims to justify strict new voting policies.

On Friday, the three Republican board members sought to cast the changes as both procedural and necessary to ensure the integrity of state elections, echoing Mr. Trump’s arguments.

“It’s a ballot security issue to make sure the voter’s will and intent is being followed through,” Stacy “Four” Eggers, a Republican member of the board, said at the virtual meeting on Friday.

In part because of such claims, Democrats in recent years have voted by mail in higher numbers than Republicans, meaning that restrictions to mail voting are more likely to disenfranchise Democrats than Republicans. Mr. Trump has stated publicly that he believes restricting the practice would benefit his party in the fall midterms.

In North Carolina, roughly 5 percent of voters cast their ballots by mail in the 2024 presidential election, a far lower rate than many other states. But with a Senate race that could help determine which party controls the chamber, small margins could make the difference.

As of Friday afternoon, election officials in the state had shipped more than 47,000 absentee ballots, according to Jason Tyson, a spokesman for the state elections board. More than 42 percent of voters who requested the ballots were registered Democrats, according to preliminary data provided by Mr. Tyson. About 38 percent of the voters were unaffiliated; more than 18 percent were Republicans.

Democrats in the state, including those on the board of elections, argued that the changes sow confusion and could disenfranchise voters with disabilities or without internet access. They also criticized the Republicans for pushing through a new rule just nine weeks ahead of Election Day.

“North Carolina voters deserve transparency in their elections, not last-minute workarounds that could keep their vote from counting,” said Governor Josh Stein, a Democrat, in a statement. “I will continue to stand up for voters’ access to the ballot box.”

One of the Democratic members of the board, Jeff Carmon, appeared at the Friday meeting with a virtual background that depicted John Lewis, the late civil rights leader. The other, Siobhan Millen, criticized her Republican counterparts for characterizing the new rules as simply technical changes.

“This does affect the voter,” she said. “It affects whether your ballot counts. That’s huge. So an effort to say this is just a process thing, I think is incorrect.”

The new rules specify that in most cases, only a voter’s “near relative” or legal guardian can deliver their mail-in ballot in person on their behalf. If election officials find that the envelope is not adequately sealed and the voter is not present to do so, the rule requires county board staff to discard the ballot and issue a new one.

The board had voted earlier this summer to approve a broader array of changes that would have made it easier to discard certain ballots. But enough state residents filed written objections to trigger a process under state law that gives the final say to the state legislature.

The board’s action on Friday amounted to an administrative directive, which is a workaround allowing changes to election practices even as a more formal and expanded version of the rules has stalled in the General Assembly.

item.title: Postal Service Internal Watchdog Opens Inquiry After Whistle-Blower’s Complaint
item.description:
The U.S. Postal Service’s internal watchdog is opening an investigation into concerns raised in a whistle-blower report about the agency’s hasty effort to build a complex online system with voter data ahead of the midterm elections.

The online portal is intended to be an additional layer of screening for mail voting that President Trump called for in a March executive order. A whistle-blower said the system designed by the Postal Service had not gone through rigorous testing and could lead to substantial delays in voters’ receiving mail ballots.

Tara Linne, a spokeswoman for the Postal Service’s inspector general, said the office had received the whistle-blower report.

“We are currently analyzing the information and plan to conduct an independent review of these allegations,” Ms. Linne said in a statement Friday afternoon.

The executive order is facing several legal challenges, and its implementation has been indefinitely paused.

Most recently, the Postal Service said this voter data portal — an online system for states to upload information about voters receiving mail ballots — would be ready for use next week on a voluntary basis.

In a statement on Friday, the postmaster general, David P. Steiner, acknowledged the whistle-blower’s concerns about the pace of the project.

“Although development proceeded on an accelerated schedule, our standards for quality, security, and system integrity were not compromised,” Mr. Steiner said. “Testing and validation have been continuous throughout the development life cycle, and our process requires that deployment be delayed whenever significant defects or security vulnerabilities are identified, until those issues are appropriately resolved.”

Mr. Steiner said the additional screening of mail ballots was a necessary security measure to “facilitate enforcement of federal law and address concerns about election integrity.”

Mr. Trump has repeatedly promoted false claims of widespread mail-in voting fraud, even as he voted by mail in two elections this year.

item.title: Judge Will Not Block Pentagon Move to Fire Stars and Stripes Journalists
item.description:
A federal judge in Washington will not immediately block the Pentagon’s move to fire three journalists at the federally funded but independent military news organization Stars and Stripes.

The ruling is an opening victory for the Pentagon’s efforts to exert control over the newspaper, which started publishing during the Civil War and has a long history of independent reporting.

Erik A. Slavin, the paper’s editor in chief; Lara S. Korte, its Middle East correspondent; and Max D. Lederer Jr., the paper’s publisher, accused the government of violating their First Amendment right to free speech. They asked the court to reject their terminations as well as new Pentagon policies that they say severely limit the editorial independence of their work.

The journalists also said their firings were related to their coverage of the worsening conditions on the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, a Navy aircraft carrier that had been deployed to the Middle East for over nine months.

In July, CBS News interviewed Mr. Slavin and Ms. Korte for a news segment on accusations of editorial interference at Stars and Stripes. Mr. Lederer, who had given Mr. Slavin and Ms. Korte permission for the CBS interview, refused to fire them despite the Pentagon’s urging. Amid continued pressure, Mr. Lederer announced that he would soon retire and issued public statements on his strife with the Defense Department’s leadership. He was then served a termination notice.

In a hearing on Friday morning, Taryn Wilgus Null, a lawyer with Democracy Defenders Fund representing the Stars and Stripes employees, argued that her clients were speaking as “private citizens about a matter of public concern,” and therefore, their comments deserved the full protection of the First Amendment.

In a 24-page ruling, Judge Trevor N. McFadden of the Federal District Court in Washington reasoned that the public remarks by Mr. Slavin, Ms. Korte and Mr. Lederer “suggest that they spoke as part of their official duties and not as private citizens.” “They are thus unlikely to succeed on the merits of their First Amendment claim,” he wrote.

The Times would like to hear about your experience as a federal worker under the second Trump administration. We may reach out about your submission, but we will not publish any part of your response without contacting you first.

Judge McFadden also rejected arguments that the journalists’ firings would cause a broader chilling effect among federal workers and federally funded news organizations, writing that “public employees are (or should be) aware that they are not free to speak as they like when conducting their official duties.”

The three employees received termination notices on Aug. 21 and were given a five-day period to challenge the action. The Pentagon, however, agreed not to finalize their dismissals before Friday, a step that Judge McFadden’s decision now allows it to take.

Judge McFadden’s ruling rejected only an initial emergency order halting the personnel actions, noting that the plaintiffs had to meet “a heavy burden” of proof to have such an order approved. But Judge McFadden, who was nominated to the court by President Trump early in his first term, appeared skeptical of the lawsuit’s merits.

“Perhaps discovery will strengthen plaintiffs’ case,” Judge McFadden wrote. “But at bottom, on the current record, plaintiffs’ real complaint seems to be that they were victims of a cruel bait-and-switch. They are being fired for giving pre-approved interviews on their paper’s behalf in which they largely toed the company line. Whatever else such a scheme may violate, it does not clearly offend the First Amendment.”

Judge McFadden was also skeptical of the journalists’ argument that they were fired in retaliation for writing about the deteriorating morale on the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln.

Judge McFadden wrote that “the U.S.S. Lincoln piece was written by a reporter other than Korte, and plaintiffs do not contend that Slavin or Lederer were directly involved,” adding that “plaintiffs themselves allege that Lederer had already received criticism related to the CBS News interview before publication of the U.S.S. Lincoln story. And the Department’s declarant states that the notices for Slavin and Korte were completed on Aug. 6, also prior to the story.”

In a statement, the three Stars and Stripes employees expressed disappointment in the ruling and noted that the broader case “remains unresolved.”

“We continue to believe that the Pentagon should not be able to fire journalists for speaking out against censorship and defending the editorial independence of Stars and Stripes,” they said in the statement.

item.title: In Major Leak Hunt, Pentagon Gives Polygraph Tests to Joint Staff Members
item.description:
U.S. government investigators have taken the extraordinary step of subjecting roughly 50 members of the U.S. military’s Joint Staff to polygraph tests over leaks to journalists, including about how the Iran war has created a shortage of crucial munitions, according to officials briefed on the move.

The investigators asked military officers and civilian employees on the Joint Staff if they disclosed classified information to members of the press, and about whether they provided information about diminished U.S. munitions stocks.

The polygraph tests were conducted in August after a flurry of news reports detailed diminished stocks of crucial munitions, including of long-range missiles and Patriot interceptors. The show of force appeared aimed at not just ferreting out anyone who may have shared information, but intimidating others who might do so in the future, according to people with knowledge of the effort.

Between 1,500 and 2,000 officers and officials work for the Joint Staff, which coordinates operations, policy and war plans with combatant commanders around the world.

In a statement, Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said that the department “does not comment on internal personnel or investigative matters but takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.”

“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” he added.

The scope of the investigation is without parallel. Mass polygraph tests have never been administered to the top ranks of the U.S. military in modern history.

“I’ve never seen polygraphs employed this broadly or at this seniority level,” said Rear Adm. Donald J. Guter, a retired top judge advocate general for the Navy from 2000 to 2002. “In my experience, it’s unprecedented.”

The move comes as multiple news organizations have revealed details about how the war with Iran has drained munition stockpiles and reported on concerns inside the administration about the strategic direction of the conflict.

President Trump has pressured administration officials to aggressively hunt for those leaking information. But the president has gone further than merely trying to stop the flow of unauthorized information; he has labeled “treasonous” the media coverage that is critical of the U.S. handling of the war in Iran and the shortages of munitions.

The leaks have intensified an atmosphere of deep distrust and paranoia inside the Pentagon, one that current and former officials say has been fostered by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Surrounded by a tight inner circle of loyalists, Mr. Hegseth has pushed out or blocked the promotions of at least 80 generals, admirals and other officials during his tenure. Since early last year, the Pentagon has been conducting a number of leak investigations in response to news coverage about his leadership, even as he faced criticism for sharing sensitive details about strikes in Yemen in a Signal group last year.

Mr. Hegseth has not given a briefing to the Pentagon press corps about the U.S. war in Iran since May 5 and has sought to limit the access of journalists at the Pentagon, a policy that The New York Times has challenged in court.

Last month, the Defense Department fired the publisher and the editor in chief of Stars and Stripes, a government-funded news outlet that reports on the U.S. military, a move the journalists said was retribution for their coverage of the worsening conditions on the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln.

Mr. Trump has stood by Mr. Hegseth, saying he is doing a “fantastic job,” despite growing concerns about the leadership turmoil inside the Pentagon.

Recently, some Republicans on Capitol Hill have begun publicly voicing criticism of the Pentagon secretary, saying he is mistreating top officials.

“I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina and a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee, wrote in a social media post this week, calling on Mr. Trump to replace Mr. Hegseth.

“He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and well-being of our fighting force,” Mr. Tillis said.

Mr. Tillis was among the senators who voted to confirm Mr. Hegseth for the role in early 2025, despite having voiced concerns about his nomination.

Greg Jaffe contributed reporting.

item.title: Former Kentucky Governor Is Arrested Amid Child Support Battle
item.description:
Matthew Bevin, a former governor of Kentucky, was arrested on Thursday after resisting court orders in a legal dispute over child support payments, the authorities said.

Mr. Bevin, a Republican who was governor from 2015 until 2019, was picked up while on a movie set after a judge issued an arrest warrant, officials said.

The judge, Angela J. Johnson of Jefferson County Family Court, had ordered Mr. Bevin to turn over documents disclosing his income and assets to finalize child support payments to his son Jonah Bevin.

But Mr. Bevin, 59, has repeatedly failed to file those papers, John Helmers Jr., a lawyer for Jonah Bevin, said on Friday.

“There is profound sadness in that Jonah must watch his father choose jail over fulfilling his obligations to support his son,” Mr. Helmers and a co-counsel for Jonah, Melina Hettiaratchi, said in a news release. “Jonah did not seek this public conflict.”

A lawyer who was representing Mr. Bevin as of March could not be reached. It was not immediately clear on Friday if Mr. Bevin had other legal representation.

Mr. Bevin was in custody at the Louisville Metro Department of Corrections as of Friday afternoon, according to the department’s website.

Mr. Helmers said that a date for Mr. Bevin to appear in court had not yet been set.

The child support dispute stems from a divorce filing in 2023 involving Mr. Bevin and his former wife, Glenna Bevin.

Jonah Bevin intervened in the proceedings seeking child support after he argued that he had been mistreated.

The couple adopted Jonah, who is now 19, from Ethiopia when he was 5 years old.

Judge Johnson last year ordered Mr. Bevin to turn over documents detailing his assets and income to determine how much child support he must pay, Mr. Helmers said.

The former governor turned over some papers, but they were redacted, prompting Judge Johnson to request that Mr. Bevin refile his financial disclosures, Mr. Helmers said.

Mr. Bevin did not do so.

He was held in contempt this year by Judge Johnson after he failed to furnish the documents, Mr. Helmers said.

In June, Judge Johnson held Mr. Bevin in contempt of court for a second time, issued a warrant for his arrest, fined him $500 and sentenced him to 60 days in jail, Mr. Helmers said.

“These are routine financial documents that are ordered by everyone to file in divorce” proceedings, Mr. Helmers said, adding that, “It’s highly unorthodox for people not to comply with routine court orders.”

The Bourbon County Sheriff’s Office said in a news release on Friday that it had received a call at about 5:30 p.m. on Thursday that Mr. Bevin was participating in a movie being filmed in Kentucky.

Deputies arrived at the film set and took Mr. Bevin into custody “without any issues,” the sheriff’s office said.

On Thursday, the Great American Family, a cable television network that produces family-friendly programming, according to its website, was filming its latest Christmas film, “The Greatest Christmas Gift” in Paris, Ky., The Lexington Herald-Leader reported.

Mr. Bevin was appearing in the movie as an extra, the newspaper reported.

A representative for the network said on Friday that it was unaware of Mr. Bevin’s arrest.

Sheelagh McNeill contributed research.

item.title: Appeals Court Maintains Block on Federal Voter Identification Tool
item.description:
A federal appeals court panel declined late Friday to let the Department of Homeland Security restore access to a new tool that would allow states to compare their voter rolls against federal citizenship and Social Security data.

By a 2-1 vote, a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit determined that the department had not shown that the new system, built out of a database historically used to check the legal status of immigrants, could be done without violating privacy laws protecting Social Security information.

The ruling kept the system offline for now as the Trump administration has launched an all- out legal effort to put in place new restrictions on voting in time for the midterm elections in November.

Chief Judge Sri Srinivasan and Judge Robert L. Wilkins, appointees of President Obama, formed the majority. Judge Gregory G. Katsas, an appointee of President Trump, wrote in a dissenting opinion that he would have lifted a lower court’s order blocking the department from making the tool available.

“The public interest does not favor interim restoration of a system the government has not made a strong showing it may lawfully operate,” the majority’s opinion said.

The ruling was temporary, and the judges on the panel said that they would reach a full decision on the underlying legal questions within 10 days.

The database at issue was created at President Trump’s direction in an executive order giving federal agencies a more direct role policing elections. In addition to the Homeland Security tool, the order also ordered the Postal Service to take steps to check the eligibility of voters casting ballots by mail.

Earlier on Friday, a federal judge in Massachusetts blocked the Postal Service from making those changes. But the Trump administration has continued to fight adverse rulings and push for both agencies to be allowed to implement the new processes in time for the upcoming election, now less than 60 days away.

A lower court judge had ruled in June that repurposing the modified citizenship database for use in election monitoring violated several federal laws prohibiting the disclosure of sensitive federal data.

The majority noted that the Trump administration had waited until after the case was decided to put forward novel arguments about why the Social Security data could be used in the database, which the lower court had not had an opportunity to consider.

The earlier ruling in June also drew a parallel lawsuit by Republican-led states, which sued in Florida seeking to regain access to the database to screen their voter rolls for possible noncitizens. In July, a federal judge in that case agreed, ordering that officials in Florida, Ohio, Iowa and Indiana be allowed to access the Homeland Security data once again.

item.title: In Red States, Law-and-Order Republicans Turn Against Flock Cameras
item.description:
The Texas governor, Greg Abbott, directed police departments last week to stop spending state money on Flock Safety cameras, the license-plate readers that have drawn bipartisan backlash around the country.

Days later in Florida, Gov. Ron DeSantis’s administration ordered the systems removed from state roads. Mr. DeSantis has described the surveillance technology as “out of control.”

Both governors are tough-on-crime Republicans with deep backing from law enforcement agencies. Yet their moves underscore how the political winds are shifting against Flock and other plate-reading systems that have been embraced by police departments.

The cameras, which began rapidly appearing by the tens of thousands on American roads in recent years, track vehicles and feed surveillance databases. The networks of cameras can be used to assist officers by quickly locating vehicles connected with crimes. But concerns about a sweeping system of government surveillance and about abuses by individual officers have brought mounting opposition.

Flock cameras and others like them have become a campaign issue in several states, in some cases uniting Republicans and Democrats.

The result of the actions in Texas and Florida: Police departments are falling in line behind their governors and dismantling their license-plate readers. They have begun doing so even as they extol the cameras’ crime-fighting capabilities. In Jacksonville, Fla., the sheriff, a Republican, announced on Monday he was pausing his agency’s program of 150 cameras — one week after the office released a documentary-style video lauding their role in solving a kidnapping, among other crimes.

The moves in Texas and Florida are unfolding as Republican elected officials elsewhere are mulling their own restrictions.

In Indiana, Republicans have signaled they will draft legislation to set minimum law enforcement standards for the technology. In Kansas, some Republican lawmakers now say they want to tighten restrictions and oversight after earlier legislation had made it easier for the police to deploy license-plate readers.

In Tennessee, the state chapter of Americans for Prosperity, which has backed some of the state’s top Republicans, celebrated a unanimous Knox County Commission vote this week to remove Flock cameras. The ordinance was signed by the outgoing mayor, Glenn Jacobs, a Republican better known as the wrestler Kane.

Barry Friedman, a professor at the New York University School of Law and the director of its Policing Project, said he is not surprised conservatives are realizing the perils of the rapidly deployed technology.

“I can’t imagine what would be a greater affront to conservatives than the government spying on multitudes of blameless people,” Mr. Friedman said.

Democratic leaders have also taken steps to address concerns. In Columbus, Ohio, for example, Mayor Andrew Ginther paused the city’s Flock program this week to investigate potential misuse by an officer. Los Angeles has also paused its use of the cameras.

Although several companies have contracts with police departments for license-plate readers, Flock has attracted the most vitriol, in part because of the size of its network. Its contracts with 7,000 law enforcement agencies cover nearly every state. The company has more than 100,000 cameras feeding into its vast database.

Some officers have abused their access to the information collected by the cameras. In East Texas, an officer was accused of using Flock more than 10,000 times to track his ex-girlfriend and others. Mr. Abbott’s office cited the case to support halting state spending on Flock cameras.

A Flock spokesman said its technology was an important public safety tool and that it supported bipartisan legislation “that puts strong privacy, transparency, and accountability guardrails in place.”

The Dallas Police Department said 321 of its Flock cameras would be deactivated, though at least 300 others will remain in use because they were not purchased with state funds. Several smaller Texas cities said they were stopping their Flock programs.

Mitch Little, a Republican state representative in a North Texas district, said he would consider a ban on Flock cameras despite their popularity with the police. “That’s really not the job of the Legislature to make law enforcement’s job easier,” Mr. Little said.

Mr. DeSantis, who frequently hails his state as a conservative bastion, said his concern was over the extent of the surveillance.

“What we don’t want in the state of Florida is to have a digital A.I. surveillance state where everything we’re doing is being tracked at all times,” Mr. DeSantis told reporters.

While Florida police officials have mostly avoided directly criticizing Mr. DeSantis, Sheriff Bill Prummell of Charlotte County, in southwest Florida, said “criminals are jumping up and down for joy” at the state’s order.

Sheriff Prummell criticized the “knee-jerk reactions to something that really isn’t a problem,” and said the response ignored the benefits of the technology.

Although the order applies only to state roads, departments in communities like Jacksonville and Miami-Dade County suspended their entire programs.

Not all Florida departments were pausing their programs. Sheriffs in Polk and Orange Counties, in Greater Orlando, said they will operate cameras on nonstate roads.

“Technology already knows everything about all of us,” Sheriff Grady Judd of Polk County said. “What we have to do in government is to make sure that it’s used appropriately.”

Emily Cochrane contributed reporting.
